newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-ABB picks new CEO, Barnevik remains.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-ABB picks new CEO, Barnevik remains.

text.p: Percy Barnevik, one of Europe's leading industrialists, is handing over responsibility for daily operations of ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG to fellow Swede Goran Lindahl, the electrical engineering group said on Thursday.

Barnevik, who has transformed ABB into one of the world's most respected companies, will remain chairman but focus on ABB's external relations, customer contacts and board memberships in other firms and organisations.
Industry analysts welcomed the move because it ensured that ABB's successful strategy would be continued.
"This is more of a fine-tuning within management than a change in direction and philosophy of the company," said Klas Anderson of Goldman Sachs International.
At a joint news conference, Barnevik and Lindahl stressed the continuity of ABB's corporate culture and said that management of the $36-billion global group was already very decentralised.
"Barnevik was the figure head, but ABB was always more than Barnevik," said one London-based analyst.
The naming of a new chief executive from January 1, 1997, had been expected since February, when Barnevik, 55, temporarily took over both roles as part of a restructuring of its board.
"I believe one should not combine supervision and the executive in the same person because then you supervise yourself," a good-humoured Barnevik told a news conference.
Barnevik has been the visionary chief executive and president of ABB since 1988, when it was created by the merger of Sweden's Asea AB and Switzerland's BBC Brown Boveri AG.

The merger -- now considered one of the most successful cross-border mergers -- created an international group that has aggressively expanded in Asia and Central Europe while strengthening its European basis.
The succession of Barnevik was handled smoothly said Angela Dean of Morgan Stanley but stock markets were less enthusiastic about the move, which mystified some dealers.
On the Swiss Exchange ABB's shares were down four francs to 1,552 francs in afternoon trading. But the entire market was lower.
"I can't understand why people are selling because this is good news," said one Zurich dealer. "Lindahl comes form a very successful division. All in all this is very positive," he said.

Analysts, however, said a short-term negative reaction by markets was to be expected because of Barnevik's charisma, which attracted investors to a company whose engineering business is less sexy and fashionable than mobile phones, for example.
Analysts said the move would not alter their positive views about ABB's earnings prospects, but added it is very difficult to anticipate how ABB could change long-term under Lindahl.
Lindahl, 51 is currently executive vice president in charge of ABB's Power Transmission and Distribution Segment and the Middle East and North Africa Region.
Lindahl is a product of the electrical engineering industry and has been with Asea since 1971. He considers himself to be technological and market oriented.
But in contrast to Barnevik, who feels at home in the U.S. and Eastern Europe, Lindahl has a strong background in Latin America and Asia.

Lindahl said he would move faster into emerging markets. In Latin America, for example, he said ABB should be able to increase annual sales to between $3.0 and 3.5 billion over the next four to five years from $1.8 billion currently.
